meta.name: Matt Pocock skills map
meta.tagline: Skills for real engineers: small, composable, not vibe coding.
meta.countNote: 27 skills in the plugin.json manifest (20 engineering + 7 productivity). Skipped: skills/misc/*, skills/in-progress/* (not in the manifest; the misc ones are frozen per .out-of-scope/frozen-misc-skills.md).

stages.name: Plan
stages.principle: Matt's pack is **built for this stage**. The rule: ==agree what to build before any code==, using hard interviews, then write it down.
when: When an idea is fuzzy → you are in Plan: start with /grill-with-docs
When the answer is in someone else's head → you are in Plan: /to-questionnaire
When the job is too big for one session → you are in Plan: /wayfinder

sources.label: README (#1 The agent didn't do what I want)

stages.name: Design
stages.principle: Settle the **shape** before building: answer questions with throwaway code, and fix the project's **words** and **modules**. ==Words first, shape second.==
when: When a question needs a runnable answer → you are in Design: /prototype
When a word means two things → you are in Design: /domain-modeling
When a module's shape is unclear → you are in Design: /codebase-design

stages.name: Build
stages.principle: Build in **small test-first steps**. ==Tests come first, one slice at a time.== Bugs get a feedback loop before any guess.
when: When you have a ticket → you are in Build: /implement
When you have a whole spec → you are in Build: /implement-spec
When a hard bug appears → you are in Build: /diagnosing-bugs

stages.name: Test
stages.principle: Testing itself happens **inside Build** (/tdd). This stage is the **review**: ==check the whole change against standards and the spec==.
when: When a branch is done → you are in Test: /code-review
When /implement finishes → /code-review already runs for you
stages.gap: No separate QA, e2e or browser-testing skill. Tests live in /tdd (Build). The review is /code-review.

stages.name: Deploy
stages.principle: Get the change out: a clear **pull request**, and a script for the ==steps only a human can do==.
when: When you open a pull request → you are in Deploy: /pr
When you must set secrets or do a cutover by hand → you are in Deploy: /wizard
stages.gap: No CI/CD, release, or rollout skill. /pr and /wizard are the only shipping helpers.

stages.name: Maintain
stages.principle: Keep it healthy: **sort new issues**, **learn from sessions**, and ==check the code's shape every few days==.
when: When issues pile up → you are in Maintain: /triage
When a session went badly → you are in Maintain: /retro
When you have spare time → you are in Maintain: /improve-codebase-architecture
stages.gap: No monitoring, logs, metrics or incident skill. Maintenance is about issues, agent setup and code shape.

categories.name: Get answers you lack
categories.blurb: Look things up, or ask the person who knows.
categories.principle: If the answer is **not in your head**, go get it. ==Facts are the agent's job; decisions are yours.==
when: When you need facts from docs or code → start with research
When the answer is in someone else's head → start with to-questionnaire
categories.chainWhy: Both are standalone and feed /grill-with-docs (ask-matt Standalone). The two are independent; their order here is inferred.

categories.name: Sharpen the idea into tickets
categories.blurb: The main flow: grill, write the spec, split into tickets.
categories.principle: One unbroken thread: ==grill → spec → tickets==. Keep one context window until the tickets exist.
when: When you have an idea in a repo → start with grill-with-docs
When the grilling is done and the build spans sessions → to-spec
When you have a spec → to-tickets
categories.chainWhy: ask-matt main flow steps 1 and 3 give this order. Context hygiene says do not compact or clear until after /to-tickets (ask-matt L36-38).

categories.name: Chart a huge foggy job
categories.blurb: For work too big for one session.
categories.principle: When the way is not visible, ==make decisions first, build later==. Hand off to /to-spec.
when: When the job is too big for one session → start with wayfinder
When the map is clear → to-spec
categories.chainWhy: ask-matt L52-54: when the map clears, it hands off at /to-spec, not /implement.

categories.name: Try it with throwaway code
categories.blurb: Answer a design question by building a quick demo.
categories.principle: When a question can't be settled by talking, ==build a cheap thing and look at it==.
when: When a question needs a runnable answer → hand off, then prototype
When the prototype answers it → hand the lesson back
categories.chainWhy: ask-matt step 2 (L20-23): handoff out, prototype, handoff back. The chain shows the first two; the return handoff is the third step.

categories.name: Pick the words and the shape
categories.blurb: Clean up the project's words and its modules.
categories.principle: Good names and deep modules make everything after easier. ==Words first, shape second.==
when: When a word means two things → start with domain-modeling
When a module's shape is unclear → codebase-design
categories.chainWhy: Both sit 'underneath' other skills (ask-matt L62-67). Order is inferred: the glossary words name the seams.

categories.name: Build one piece
categories.blurb: One ticket or one small job, test-first.
categories.principle: Build **one slice at a time** and review before commit. ==Clear the context between tickets.==
when: When you have a ticket or small job → start with implement
When you want only test-first code → use tdd alone
categories.chainWhy: implement/SKILL.md L11: calls tdd where possible, at pre-agreed seams.

categories.name: Build the whole spec
categories.blurb: Parallel helpers on one integration branch.
categories.principle: Treat tickets as a **graph**, not a list. ==Run everything ready at once.==
when: When you want to orchestrate the whole spec → start with implement-spec
categories.chainWhy: implement-spec/SKILL.md L29: each implementer calls tdd for its ticket.

categories.name: Fix a hard bug
categories.blurb: Make the bug fail on demand, then fix it.
categories.principle: Don't guess. ==First make a tight loop that goes red on this bug.==
when: When a bug resists a first look → start with diagnosing-bugs
When the cause is found → add the regression test with tdd
categories.chainWhy: diagnosing-bugs Phase 5 (L114) fixes with a regression test. Naming tdd as the next step is inferred.

categories.name: Check the change
categories.blurb: Review the diff against standards and spec.
categories.principle: Review with fresh eyes. ==Two reviewers, two questions: follows the standards? matches the spec?==
when: When a branch or PR needs review → start with code-review
categories.chainWhy: One skill. /implement and /implement-spec call it for you (implement L15; implement-spec L36).

categories.name: Open the pull request
categories.blurb: A clear PR body with proof.
categories.principle: A PR should show **what changed, that it works, and how risky it is**. ==Smallest picture that makes it clear.==
when: When you open a pull request → use pr
categories.chainWhy: One skill; model-invoked whenever a PR is written (ask-matt L32).

categories.name: Do the human-only steps
categories.blurb: Scripts for secrets, dashboards and cutovers.
categories.principle: If only a human can do it, ==give them a wizard==, not an essay.
when: When you must set secrets or credentials → use wizard
When a one-off migration needs a human → use wizard
categories.chainWhy: One skill; model-invoked when the agent hits a wall only you can pass (ask-matt L90).

categories.name: Sort new issues
categories.blurb: Turn raw reports into agent-ready work.
categories.principle: Raw reports need a **label and a brief**. ==Only triage issues you didn't create.==
when: When bugs and requests pile up → use triage
When an issue is ready-for-agent → implement
categories.chainWhy: ask-matt L46: triage produces agent-ready issues that /implement later picks up.

categories.name: Look back and tidy up
categories.blurb: Improve the agent's setup and the code's shape.
categories.principle: After a session, **fix the environment**; every few days, ==fix the code's shape==.
when: When a session went badly or a bug is fixed → start with retro
When retro says there is no good seam → improve-codebase-architecture
categories.chainWhy: ask-matt L50: after a fix, run /retro; if the finding is a missing seam, that is a job for /improve-codebase-architecture.

anytime.name: Router
anytime.blurb: The front door. Tell it your situation and it names the skills.

anytime.name: Set up once
anytime.blurb: Run once per repo before the engineering skills.

anytime.name: Interview and re-explain
anytime.blurb: Hard questions in, plain words out. Used inside many other skills.

anytime.name: Learn and write
anytime.blurb: Learn a topic; write docs agents can read.

ask-matt.name: ask-matt
when: When you **do not remember** which skill to use → [[ask-matt]]
When you have an idea and want it **built, end to end** → [[ask-matt]]
When you are **stuck between** two flows and want a ==pick== for your situation → [[ask-matt]]
ask-matt.whatItIs: It is the **front desk**. You tell it your situation and it points you to the right skill or flow.
howItWorks: It knows one **main flow**: idea → grill → (prototype) → spec → tickets → implement → review → retro
It knows **on-ramps**: triage, diagnosing-bugs, wayfinder
It reads the skill's own file **before** it recommends or skips a step
It also says when to **continue, clear, handoff, use a subagent, or compact**

example.situation: You have a half-formed idea for a new billing page and no idea where to start.
example.youType: /ask-matt I want to add a billing page. Where do I start?
whatHappens: It checks it is a repo, so it picks /grill-with-docs (not /grill-me).
It asks whether any question needs a runnable answer, which would mean a prototype.
It asks if the build is multi-session, which would mean /to-spec then /to-tickets.
example.youGet: A short **path** of skills to run, in order, for your job.

behindTheScenes: pick main flow, on-ramp, or standalone

setup-matt-pocock-skills.name: setup-matt-pocock-skills
when: When you **install the pack** in a new repo → [[setup-matt-pocock-skills]]
When you want to **switch issue trackers** → [[setup-matt-pocock-skills]]
When a skill says =="run setup"== because it has no tracker → [[setup-matt-pocock-skills]]
setup-matt-pocock-skills.whatItIs: A **one-time setup**. It tells the other skills where your tickets, labels and docs live.
howItWorks: It asks which **issue tracker** you use: GitHub, GitLab, local files, or your own
It asks what **labels** you put on tickets (only if triage is installed)
It asks where **domain docs** go: one context or several
It writes notes into `docs/agents/*.md` and a short pointer in your agent file

example.situation: Fresh repo, you just installed the pack.
whatHappens: It asks GitHub or local files.
example.youGet: `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md`, `domain.md`, and `triage-labels.md`, which the other skills read.

grilling.name: grilling
when: When you want the **raw interview** with no wrapper → [[grilling]]
When another skill needs to **stress-test a plan** → [[grilling]]
When you say =="grill me"== and name no special mode → [[grilling]]
grilling.whatItIs: The **interview engine**. It asks hard questions, in rounds, until nothing is left unsaid.
howItWorks: It draws a **tree** of decisions; each answer opens new questions
Each round it asks every question it can ask **right now**, with its own suggested answer
It looks up **facts** itself; you only decide
It stops when **no questions are left**, then waits for your OK

example.situation: You are unsure how a feature should work.
whatHappens: Round 1: 5 numbered questions, each with a suggested answer.
You say yes or fix a few.
Round 2 only asks what the answers unlocked.

grilling.invoked: the agent can reach for it

grill-me.name: grill-me
when: When you have **no working folder** and want a plan sharpened → [[grill-me]]
When you plan a **talk, essay, or decision**, not code → [[grill-me]]
When you want the grill but ==save nothing== → [[grill-me]]
grill-me.whatItIs: The **stateless grill**. Same hard interview, but it writes no files.
howItWorks: It just runs the **grilling** skill
It builds **no glossary** and keeps no notes
Use /grill-with-docs instead when a repo exists

example.situation: You are planning a conference talk, not code.
whatHappens: It asks the frontier questions with suggested answers.
example.youGet: A **sharper plan** in the chat only.

wait-what.name: wait-what
when: When the agent's last message used **words you do not know** → [[wait-what]]
When you say =="huh?"== mid-skill → [[wait-what]]
When jargon is **piling up** → [[wait-what]]
howItWorks: You fire it right after a confusing message
The agent **re-pitches** the same point with the missing context
It uses plain English and your `GLOSSARY.md` words

example.situation: The agent said "the materialization cascade breaks idempotency".
whatHappens: It explains the term using your glossary.
It re-says the point in plain words.

teach.name: teach
when: When you want to **learn a concept** over several days → [[teach]]
When you want a **stateful** study folder → [[teach]]
When you ==learn by doing== rather than reading → [[teach]]
teach.whatItIs: A **tutor** that uses the current folder as your study workspace and remembers where you left off.
howItWorks: It keeps the lesson state in the folder
Each session picks up from the last
It checks what you understood before moving on

example.situation: You want to learn Rust ownership properly.
whatHappens: It starts a workspace in the folder.
It teaches a bit and checks you.
example.youGet: A **study folder** with progress you can resume.

writing-for-agents.name: writing-for-agents
when: When you **write or edit a skill** → [[writing-for-agents]]
When you change **AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md** → [[writing-for-agents]]
When an agent reads a doc because ==another file points to it== → [[writing-for-agents]]
writing-for-agents.whatItIs: A **style guide** for writing things an agent will read.
howItWorks: It is model-invoked, so the agent loads it by itself while writing agent docs
It says what to put in always-loaded files and what to point to instead
/retro uses it too

example.situation: Your AGENTS.md has grown to 600 lines.
whatHappens: It moves detail into pointed-at docs.

writing-for-agents.invoked: the agent can reach for it

research.name: research
when: When you need **facts from official docs or source code** → [[research]]
When you want to **keep working** while it reads → [[research]]
When you want a ==cited file== to feed your grilling → [[research]]
research.whatItIs: A **background reader**. It checks the real sources and leaves a Markdown file with citations.
howItWorks: It starts a **background agent**
The agent reads **primary sources** only: docs, source, specs
It writes one file and cites every claim
You take the file into /grill-with-docs

example.situation: You are unsure how a payment API handles retries.
whatHappens: A background agent reads Stripe's docs.
example.youGet: A **cited Markdown file** in the repo.

research.invoked: the agent can reach for it

to-questionnaire.name: to-questionnaire
when: When the answer is **in someone else's head** → [[to-questionnaire]]
When you must ask a **boss, client or expert** → [[to-questionnaire]]
When you want to ==send questions== they fill in later → [[to-questionnaire]]
to-questionnaire.whatItIs: It turns **your open question** into a Markdown form for the one person who knows.
howItWorks: It does **not** quiz you about the subject
It quizzes you about the **send**: who gets it, what you need back
It writes questions aimed at the gap
The answers come back as input for /grill-with-docs or /to-spec

example.situation: You need pricing rules only the finance lead knows.
example.youType: /to-questionnaire pricing rules for the new plan
whatHappens: It asks who reads it and what you need.

grill-with-docs.name: grill-with-docs
when: When you have an **idea in a repo** and want it sharp → [[grill-with-docs]]
When words in the project are **fuzzy or overloaded** → [[grill-with-docs]]
When you start ==any change== and want a paper trail → [[grill-with-docs]]
grill-with-docs.whatItIs: The **start of the main flow**. A hard interview that also writes your glossary and decision notes.
howItWorks: It runs two skills: **grilling** (the questions) and **domain-modeling** (the words)
Fuzzy terms get fixed in `GLOSSARY.md`
Hard-to-undo choices become short ADR notes
Do this before spec, tickets, or code

example.situation: You want "teams" in your app but the code already uses "team" for two things.
whatHappens: It notices "team" is overloaded and proposes two words.
It updates GLOSSARY.md as you agree.
example.youGet: A **shared plan** plus an updated glossary and ADRs.

to-spec.name: to-spec
when: When the grilling is **done** and the build spans sessions → [[to-spec]]
When you want a **written spec** on your tracker → [[to-spec]]
When a wayfinder map is ==clear== → [[to-spec]]
to-spec.whatItIs: It **writes down** what you already agreed as a spec. It asks no new questions.
howItWorks: It reads the repo and uses your glossary words
It picks **test seams** (as few as one) and checks them with you
It fills a template: problem, solution, user stories, decisions, testing, out of scope
It publishes the spec labeled `ready-for-agent`

example.situation: You finished grilling the billing page idea.
whatHappens: It posts the spec to the tracker.

to-tickets.name: to-tickets
when: When you have a **spec or plan** and need small jobs → [[to-tickets]]
When work must be split so each piece **ships alone** → [[to-tickets]]
When each job must ==say what must finish first== → [[to-tickets]]
to-tickets.whatItIs: It slices a plan into **small jobs that each work end to end**, and each says what must finish first.
howItWorks: Each ticket cuts through **every layer** and fits one fresh context
Each names the tickets that **block** it
It shows you the list and asks about size and order
On a real tracker blocking becomes native links; locally, one file per ticket

example.situation: The billing spec is big.
example.youGet: A **set of tickets** with blocking edges.

wayfinder.name: wayfinder
when: When the job is **too big for one session** → [[wayfinder]]
When you cannot yet **see the way** from here to done → [[wayfinder]]
When it is a ==greenfield or huge feature==, not a normal one → [[wayfinder]]
wayfinder.whatItIs: It draws a **map of decisions** on your tracker and clears them one by one. It makes decisions, not code.
howItWorks: You name the **destination** first
It files **decision tickets**: questions, prototypes, research, tasks
You resolve them one at a time as the fog lifts
When clear it **hands off to /to-spec**, not to /implement

example.situation: You must rebuild the whole auth system over weeks.
example.youType: /wayfinder move us from sessions to OAuth
example.youGet: A **cleared map** of decisions, ready for /to-spec.

triage.name: triage
when: When **bug reports pile up** → [[triage]]
When strangers file raw feature requests → [[triage]]
When you ask ==what is ready for agents?== → [[triage]]
triage.whatItIs: It moves **raw issues** through simple labels until each is ready for an agent or a human.
howItWorks: Each issue gets one **category** (bug or enhancement) and one **state**
States: needs-triage, needs-info, ready-for-agent, ready-for-human, wontfix
It checks the claim, grills you if needed, and writes an agent brief
Do not triage tickets that /to-tickets made

example.situation: 20 new issues arrived over the weekend.
example.youType: /triage show me anything that needs my attention
whatHappens: It lists unlabeled, stale, and waiting issues.
It verifies the bug and labels ready-for-agent.

handoff.name: handoff
when: When you go to a **new tool, folder or person** → [[handoff]]
When you **fork a side job** mid-phase → [[handoff]]
When you want to carry a prototype's lesson ==back== → [[handoff]]
handoff.whatItIs: It packs the chat into a **short note** so a fresh agent can continue.
howItWorks: It writes to your temp folder, not the repo
It lists **suggested skills** for the next agent
It points to specs, issues and commits instead of copying them
It hides secrets

example.situation: You need to prototype in a new folder.
example.youType: /handoff try the checkout state machine as a prototype
whatHappens: It writes a note with context and next skills.
example.youGet: A **handoff file** to open in a new session.

prototype.name: prototype
when: When a question needs a **runnable answer** → [[prototype]]
When you wonder if a **state model feels right** → [[prototype]]
When you ask ==what should this UI look like?== → [[prototype]]
prototype.whatItIs: A **throwaway program** that answers one design question fast.
howItWorks: Logic question → one **HTML file** you double-click
Look question → several **UI variations** on one route
No tests, no polish, state shown after every step
Keep it on a `prototype/<name>` branch as proof

example.situation: You are not sure how a cart discount stacks.
whatHappens: It builds a one-file HTML demo.
example.youGet: A **verdict** plus a prototype kept on a branch.

prototype.invoked: the agent can reach for it

domain-modeling.name: domain-modeling
when: When a **word means two things** → [[domain-modeling]]
When you write `GLOSSARY.md` or an ADR → [[domain-modeling]]
When you ==record a hard-to-undo decision== → [[domain-modeling]]
domain-modeling.whatItIs: It keeps your project's **words** clean in a glossary and short decision notes.
howItWorks: It challenges fuzzy terms and invents edge cases
It writes the term to `GLOSSARY.md` right away
It records big choices as ADRs in `docs/adr/`
/grill-with-docs drives it

example.situation: "Account" means user, billing, and login.

domain-modeling.invoked: the agent can reach for it

codebase-design.name: codebase-design
when: When you design a **module's interface** → [[codebase-design]]
When you decide **where pieces of code plug together** → [[codebase-design]]
When code must be easier to **test and navigate** → [[codebase-design]]
codebase-design.whatItIs: **Shared words for designing code**: put lots of behavior behind a small, simple door.
howItWorks: It names: module, interface, depth, seam, adapter, leverage, locality
/tdd and /improve-codebase-architecture use the same words
Use it when the shape, not the process, is the problem

example.situation: A module has 12 public functions.
whatHappens: It names the interface and its depth.

codebase-design.invoked: the agent can reach for it

implement.name: implement
when: When you have a **spec or ticket** and want code → [[implement]]
When the job is small enough for **one window** → [[implement]]
When you want it built ==test-first and reviewed== → [[implement]]
implement.whatItIs: It **builds** a spec or one ticket, then reviews and commits.
howItWorks: It fetches the ticket and says its title
It calls **/tdd** at pre-agreed seams
It runs types often, one test file often, the full suite once
It calls **/code-review**, then commits to the current branch

example.situation: Ticket #14: add the invoice email.
whatHappens: It drives /tdd, one slice at a time.
example.youGet: A **committed, reviewed change**. Use /clear before the next ticket.

implement-spec.name: implement-spec
when: When you want the **whole spec built in one run** → [[implement-spec]]
When many tickets can go **in parallel** → [[implement-spec]]
When you would rather ==be the manager== than drive each ticket → [[implement-spec]]
When you are **looping by hand**, one ticket per prompt → [[implement-spec]]
implement-spec.whatItIs: It builds a whole plan by running **helper agents** on its tickets, in the right order, on one branch.
howItWorks: It reads tickets as a **graph**; the ready ones are the frontier
Each helper works in its own worktree and calls **/tdd**
A merger agent lands each on one integration branch
At the end it runs **/code-review** over the whole branch and fixes issues

example.situation: Spec #87 was split into tickets #88 to #97; some don't depend on each other.
whatHappens: It maps which tickets wait on others.
The ready ones start in parallel, each in its own worktree.
Finished work merges; new tickets unlock.
example.youGet: One **integration branch** (and a draft PR if your tracker wants it).

tdd.name: tdd
when: When you build a **feature or fix** test-first → [[tdd]]
When you say ==red-green-refactor== → [[tdd]]
When you want tests only at **spots you agreed on** → [[tdd]]
tdd.whatItIs: The **test-first rules**: write a failing test, then just enough code to pass, one small piece at a time.
howItWorks: Agree the **seams** with you before any test
Red before green; never write all tests up front
Avoid tests tied to internals or that repeat the code's math
Cleanup belongs to review, not the loop

example.situation: Add a discount rule to checkout.
whatHappens: It makes it pass, then next slice.

tdd.invoked: the agent can reach for it

diagnosing-bugs.name: diagnosing-bugs
when: When a bug **resists a first look** → [[diagnosing-bugs]]
When it fails **sometimes** (flaky) → [[diagnosing-bugs]]
When something **used to work** and now does not → [[diagnosing-bugs]]
diagnosing-bugs.whatItIs: A **step-by-step debugging loop** that refuses to guess until it has a way to make the bug fail on demand.
howItWorks: Phase 1: build a **tight feedback loop** that goes red on this bug
Then reproduce and shrink it, make guesses, add logging
Then fix with a **regression test**, then clean up
It hides secrets in what it shows

example.situation: Checkout fails about 1 time in 20.
whatHappens: It builds a script that loops the call.
It finds the cause and adds a test.

diagnosing-bugs.invoked: the agent can reach for it

code-review.name: code-review
when: When a **branch or PR** needs review → [[code-review]]
When /implement just finished → [[code-review]]
When you ask ==review since main== → [[code-review]]
code-review.whatItIs: A **two-part review** of your changes: coding standards, and does it match the spec.
howItWorks: You give it a **fixed point** (a commit, branch or main)
It finds the spec and your written standards
Two helper agents review **in parallel**; it adds a code-smell checklist
It shows both reports side by side

example.situation: Branch done, spec is issue #9.

code-review.invoked: the agent can reach for it

pr.name: pr
when: When the agent **writes a pull request** → [[pr]]
When reviewers need to **see the change fast** → [[pr]]
When you want to know ==how risky the merge is== → [[pr]]
pr.whatItIs: The **shape of a good PR body**: a small picture, before/after proof, and how risky the merge is.
howItWorks: Summary: the smallest visual that shows the change
Evidence: before and after; **screenshots** are best, then test runs or output
Merge danger: can you **roll it back** (two-way door) or not (one-way), plus blast radius
The agent reaches for it by itself when writing a PR

example.situation: You finished a cache change and need a PR.
whatHappens: It marks it a two-way door.

pr.invoked: the agent can reach for it

wizard.name: wizard
when: When you must **set up credentials or CI secrets** → [[wizard]]
When a cutover needs **a human clicking** → [[wizard]]
When a third-party dashboard is ==unfamiliar== → [[wizard]]
wizard.whatItIs: It writes a **guided script** for steps only you can do, so you never re-explain them.
howItWorks: It reads `.env`, workflows and config to find every needed value
It builds a bash wizard: opens URLs, says what to click, captures values
It writes `.env` and GitHub secrets safely and can re-run
Only for human steps; the agent does the rest itself

example.situation: You must add 5 API keys to CI.
whatHappens: It lists each secret the workflows use.

wizard.invoked: the agent can reach for it

retro.name: retro
when: When a build **went sideways** → [[retro]]
When the fix is done and you ask ==what would have prevented this?== → [[retro]]
When you want to **improve the agent's setup** → [[retro]]
When AGENTS.md is **bloated** with rules that change nothing → [[retro]]
retro.whatItIs: It looks back at a session and suggests changes to the **environment**, not the code.
howItWorks: It reads the session log (the current one by default)
It checks 7 areas: navigation, automated checks, coding standards, AGENTS.md size, tool economy, no-op instructions, info access
Mechanical mistakes → a **lint rule, pre-commit hook or CI job**; judgement calls → CODING_STANDARDS.md
It ==presents== the fixes to you, most serious first; you pick which to apply

example.situation: The agent wasted 20 minutes finding the config file.
whatHappens: It spots a missing navigation pointer.

improve-codebase-architecture.name: improve-codebase-architecture
when: When you have a **spare moment** for upkeep → [[improve-codebase-architecture]]
When a bug showed there is **no good seam** → [[improve-codebase-architecture]]
When the code feels ==hard for agents to navigate== → [[improve-codebase-architecture]]
improve-codebase-architecture.whatItIs: A **checkup** that finds places to make modules deeper and shows them as a visual report.
howItWorks: It explores the code using your glossary and ADRs
It makes an **HTML report** of candidates
You pick one and it grills you on it
Use /codebase-design to design the pick

example.situation: The codebase has grown messy.
example.youGet: An **HTML report** and an idea for /grill-with-docs.
